title: Do parallel and equal opposite sides always make a rectangle?
description: A rectangle has opposite sides parallel and equal, and the video asks whether that alone is enough to define it. It draws two pairs of parallel lines that cross at a slant and looks at the corners of the shape they make.
teaching_notes: One idea: to show a definition fails, find a shape that has the property but is not the shape. Watch for students who take one property of a rectangle as its whole definition.

source: Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5)
video_script.why: The child knows that a rectangle has opposite sides parallel and equal, and tests whether that property alone is enough to define it.
video_script.substitution: Draw two pairs of parallel lines that cross at a slant, then check the corners of the shape they make against the four right angles of a rectangle.
video_script.anchor: a slanted four sided shape made by two pairs of parallel lines, with angles 60, 120, 60 and 120 degrees
video_script.payoff_line: No, a slanted shape can have parallel and equal opposite sides without being a rectangle

final_answer.spoken: no, a slanted shape can have parallel and equal opposite sides without being a rectangle

hold_back: a slanted shape is not a rectangle
maths_rules: a rectangle has opposite sides parallel and equal, and four angles of 90 degrees
two pairs of parallel lines crossing at 60 degrees make a four sided shape with opposite sides parallel and equal
its angles are 60, 120, 60 and 120 degrees, which add to 360 degrees
no angle is 90 degrees, so it is not a rectangle
so parallel and equal opposite sides do not define a rectangle
video_script.design: One idea: a counter example shows that a property is not a definition. The slanted shape with its four angles stays on the board.

<bookmark mark='ang'/>Its angles are sixty, one hundred twenty, sixty and one hundred twenty degrees.

beats.on_screen: Answer: No. A slanted shape is not a rectangle even when its opposite sides are parallel and equal
